explanations.explanation: Moses, Israel's leader, tells Aaron the priest to take a young bull and a ram, “…both without blemish…” (Leviticus 9:2). One rule covers both animals. That's a high bar, friend. I can't keep my own apron spotless through one batch of chocolate chip dough.

That's not in Moses' words, friend. Moses, Israel's leader, tells Aaron the priest that the young bull and the ram must be “…both without blemish…” (Leviticus 9:2). Nothing here mentions yokes or work. I'd have bet on this one too, but the verse only names one rule.

Close to a lot of things you could guess, but the verse doesn't say it. Moses, Israel's leader, tells Aaron the priest to take a young bull and a ram, “…both without blemish…” (Leviticus 9:2). Nothing about birth order comes up. The one rule for both animals is no blemish.

explanations.answer: Today the LORD will appear to them
explanations.explanation: Moses gives Aaron this line to pass on: “For today the LORD will appear to you.” (Leviticus 9:3-4). That's the whole reason, and it's a big one. I think you'd bring your best too if you knew the LORD was about to show up.

That's not the reason Moses gives here. He tells Aaron to say, “For today the LORD will appear to you.” (Leviticus 9:3-4). The reason is about the LORD appearing, not about Aaron. Good guess though, since Aaron is the one in the spotlight.

explanations.answer: Today the camp will set out
explanations.explanation: Pack the bags, friend? Not this time. Moses gives Aaron a different message to pass on: “For today the LORD will appear to you.” (Leviticus 9:4). No move is mentioned in these verses. All of those offerings are about the LORD showing up, and I'd say that's plenty of reason to get the dough ready.

The text says something different. After the offerings are brought to the front of the Tent of Meeting, “…the whole congregation drew near and stood before the LORD.” (Leviticus 9:5). That's everybody, not just Aaron and the elders. A whole crowd is standing there.

Right, friend. Leviticus 9:5 says, “…the whole congregation drew near and stood before the LORD.” It's not a private meeting for Aaron and the elders. The whole congregation is there. If this were my bakery, that's a line out the door and around the cookie planet.

That's right. Moses tells Aaron to sacrifice his own sin offering and burnt offering to make atonement for Aaron and for the people (Leviticus 9:7). So Aaron's offerings reach past Aaron. Then Moses adds the people's offering, which is also to make atonement for them.

Moses says both, friend. In Leviticus 9:7 he tells Aaron to sacrifice his own sin offering and burnt offering to make atonement for Aaron and for the people. So the people are included from the start. Then Moses adds the people's offering, which is for them as well.

Yes, the horns. Aaron's sons bring him the blood, and he dips his finger in it and applies it to the horns of the altar (Leviticus 9:9). The rest he pours out at the base of the altar. I think dipping a finger with that much riding on it takes a steady hand, and mine would be shaking.

Not the grate, friend. The verse says Aaron applies the blood to the horns of the altar (Leviticus 9:9). The grate doesn't come up in this verse at all. He does use the altar's base, but that's for the rest of the blood.
No ledge in this verse, friend. Aaron applies the blood to the horns of the altar (Leviticus 9:9). Then he pours out the rest at the base of the altar. Horns first, base last.

Right, outside the camp. The fat, the kidneys and the lobe of the liver go up in smoke on the altar, but the flesh and the hide get burned up outside the camp (Leviticus 9:10-11). So one calf ends up in two places. Same calf, two addresses.

The text sends it somewhere else, friend. Aaron burned the flesh and the hide outside the camp (Leviticus 9:11). The Tent of Meeting isn't mentioned for this part. The fat is the part that goes on the altar.

explanations.answer: At the base of the altar
explanations.explanation: The base of the altar is where Aaron poured out the rest of the blood (Leviticus 9:9). The flesh and the hide went somewhere else. He burned them outside the camp (Leviticus 9:11). Easy to mix up, since the altar is the busiest spot in the story.

Not quite, friend. The sons bring him the burnt offering “…piece by piece, including the head…” (Leviticus 9:13). Aaron's sons carry it in parts, not in one piece. Honestly, I'd want help carrying that too.
Right. Aaron's sons bring him the burnt offering “…piece by piece, including the head…” (Leviticus 9:13). Then Aaron burns them on the altar. It's a team job, and his sons are doing the carrying.

Yes. Leviticus 9:14 says, “He washed the entrails and the legs and burned them atop the burnt offering on the altar.” The washing comes first, then the burning. Even in the middle of all this, there's a step for washing.
The text says he does wash them, friend. Leviticus 9:14 says, “He washed the entrails and the legs and burned them atop the burnt offering on the altar.” So the washing happens before the burning.

Yes. Aaron took the people's male goat, slaughtered it, and “…offered it for sin like the first one.” (Leviticus 9:15). The first one was his own sin offering. So he does the same job again, this time for the people. That's the same job twice in one day. I'm tired just saying it.

Actually it's the same, friend. The text says Aaron slaughtered the people's goat and “…offered it for sin like the first one.” (Leviticus 9:15). The first one was his own sin offering. He follows the same way for the people's goat.
Not all of it, friend. Aaron “…took a handful of it, and burned it on the altar…” (Leviticus 9:17). Just a handful goes on the altar. The text doesn't say what happens to the rest.

Right. Aaron took a handful of the grain offering and burned it on the altar, in addition to the morning's burnt offering (Leviticus 9:17). Only a handful, not the whole thing. The text doesn't say what becomes of the rest.

That's it, baker. Aaron's sons bring the fat portions from the ox and the ram, and the text says they “…placed these on the breasts.” (Leviticus 9:19-20). Only after that does Aaron burn the fat portions on the altar. It's the kind of careful order I wish I'd kept in my own kitchen. I once stamped a whole tray before I rolled the dough out.

explanations.answer: On the horns of the altar
explanations.explanation: The horns got something else, friend. Earlier, Aaron applied blood to the horns of the altar (Leviticus 9:9). For the peace offering's fat portions, the text says they were placed on the breasts (Leviticus 9:20). Same altar, different job.

The grain offering was its own thing, friend. Aaron took a handful of it and burned it on the altar (Leviticus 9:17). The fat portions from the ox and the ram were placed on the breasts (Leviticus 9:20). They didn't go on the grain.

Yes. Aaron “…waved the breasts and the right thigh as a wave offering before the LORD, as Moses had commanded.” (Leviticus 9:21). The fat is burned on the altar, and these get waved. Moses had commanded it, and Aaron does what Moses said.

Outside the camp is where Aaron burned the flesh and hide of his own sin offering (Leviticus 9:11). For the breasts and the right thigh, the text says, “…he waved the breasts and the right thigh as a wave offering before the LORD, as Moses had commanded.” (Leviticus 9:21). So it's a wave, not a burn.

The elders are with Moses at the start of the story (Leviticus 9:1), but the text doesn't hand them the breasts. What it says is that Aaron “…waved the breasts and the right thigh as a wave offering before the LORD, as Moses had commanded.” (Leviticus 9:21). So the breasts and thigh get waved before the LORD.

explanations.answer: Lifts up his hands and blesses them
explanations.explanation: Yes. Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them (Leviticus 9:22). He had made the sin offering, the burnt offering and the peace offering, and then he stepped down. The blessing comes right as he finishes. I think that's a lovely way to close it out.

explanations.answer: Sends them back to their tents
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, friend. It says Aaron “…lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them.” (Leviticus 9:22). Then he steps down, and the people are still there when the glory of the LORD appears (Leviticus 9:23).

No reading here, friend. The verse says Aaron “…lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them.” (Leviticus 9:22). Moses had already told the people what the LORD commanded (Leviticus 9:6). Aaron's job right now is the blessing.
Not alone, friend. The text says, “Moses and Aaron then entered the Tent of Meeting.” (Leviticus 9:23). Both of them go in. Then both come out and bless the people.
Right. “Moses and Aaron then entered the Tent of Meeting.” (Leviticus 9:23). The two of them go in together. Then they come out and bless the people. It's more fun with two, I'd say.

explanations.answer: The burnt offering and the fat portions
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Fire came out from the presence of the LORD and consumed “…the burnt offering and the fat portions on the altar.” (Leviticus 9:24). The fire comes from the LORD's presence. When all the people saw it, they shouted for joy and fell facedown. I think that moment is one to stand still and take in.

explanations.answer: The breasts and the right thigh
explanations.explanation: Those were waved before the LORD (Leviticus 9:21). The fire from the presence of the LORD consumed “…the burnt offering and the fat portions on the altar.” (Leviticus 9:24). The breasts and the thigh aren't named there.

That's a different spot, friend. Aaron burned the flesh and the hide outside the camp (Leviticus 9:11). The fire from the LORD consumed “…the burnt offering and the fat portions on the altar.” (Leviticus 9:24).

Yes. “…when all the people saw it, they shouted for joy and fell facedown.” (Leviticus 9:24). The whole crowd sees the fire and shouts for joy. I think I'd be loud too. I get loud when a batch comes out right.
They do shout, friend. Leviticus 9:24 says, “And when all the people saw it, they shouted for joy and fell facedown.” So the shout comes first, and then they fall facedown.
